label: Homotopy Theory
notes: Begin by framing the chapter as a shift from drawing spaces to controlling deformations with algebra. The students already know paths, coverings, homology, and cohomology; this deck asks how much higher-dimensional deformation data can be made computable by exactness, cells, fibrations, and cohomology operations.

label: Chapter Map
notes: Use the dependency DAG as a reading map rather than as a prerequisite chart. Trace one route from based cubes to exact sequences, another through CW control into Whitehead, and a late route through cohomology representation, Postnikov towers, Thom classes, and Steenrod operations. The important message is that calculation appears only after structure is imposed.

label: Why Groups Are Hard
notes: Motivate the difficulty before definitions become formal. Homotopy groups of spheres look deceptively simple at the diagonal and then become irregular, range-dependent, and full of torsion phenomena. The schematic grid is deliberately original: it says that even familiar spaces produce scattered information, so the chapter teaches machines for localizing reliable information.

label: Higher Homotopy Groups
notes: Introduce higher homotopy groups through the based cube model. A class is a map from the n-cube with the entire boundary collapsed to the basepoint. Concatenation in one coordinate gives the product, and the boundary condition is what makes pasting well defined. Pause to stress that basepoints are bookkeeping, not decoration.

label: Interchange Commutativity
notes: Use the Eckmann-Hilton figure to explain why the group law changes character in dimension at least two. There are two independent concatenation directions, and the interchange law forces the two products to agree and commute. This is the first major structural simplification: higher homotopy groups are abelian.

label: Relative Homotopy
notes: Treat the relative long exact sequence as the first usable control panel. A pair keeps track of maps of cubes whose boundary lands partly in a subspace, and the boundary homomorphism records the obstruction left on that subspace. The disk-sphere check anchors the diagram in a rank-one example.

label: Whitehead Theorem
notes: State Whitehead carefully with its hypotheses visible. A weak equivalence of connected CW complexes is a homotopy equivalence, but the CW condition is doing real work: cells let one remove obstructions dimension by dimension. The figure reminds students that the theorem is not a generic statement about arbitrary spaces.

label: Cellular Approximation
notes: Build cellular approximation as a compression picture. Maps can be deformed so each skeleton lands in the corresponding skeleton, and vanishing relative groups let cells be pushed into a smaller target. This slide is the proof mechanism behind Whitehead, not a separate decorative lemma.

label: Excision Range
notes: Read the Freudenthal range grid from left to right. For an n-connected CW complex, suspension is an isomorphism below the boundary and a surjection on the boundary. The check values, sixty-four isomorphism cells and eight boundary cells, give students a concrete audit of the range convention.

label: Hurewicz Bridge
notes: Connect Hurewicz to the same computational problem as Freudenthal. Homotopy is hard, homology is computable, and under connectivity assumptions the first nonzero homotopy group maps isomorphically to homology. Ask students to notice that both range theorems give partial windows, not total formulas.

label: Fibrations Lift
notes: Present fibrations as lifting machines. The homotopy lifting property turns a homotopy downstairs into a lifted homotopy upstairs after an initial lift is chosen. This is why fibrations generate long exact sequences: lifting failures are organized as homotopy classes in the fiber.

label: Hopf Fibration
notes: Use the Hopf fibration as the geometric model that makes fibration exactness memorable. The fiber is a circle, the total space is S three, and the base is S two. The linked-fiber artifact is backed by a numerical Gauss linking value of about one, so the visual carries an invariant.

label: Cohomology Represented
notes: Move from cohomology as a group to cohomology as maps into a target space. For CW complexes, degree n cohomology with coefficients G is represented by homotopy classes of maps to K of G and n. This bridge is the reason Postnikov stages and cohomology operations can speak to each other.

label: Postnikov Tower
notes: Explain a Postnikov tower as a controlled loss of information. Each stage keeps homotopy groups only up to a certain degree, with fiber K of pi n and n. The k-invariants are the missing twisting data; they are why listing the groups alone usually does not determine the space.

label: Obstruction Logic
notes: Turn obstruction theory into a finite logic table. In the lab model, a zero obstruction lets the lift continue and a nonzero obstruction stops it at that stage. Emphasize that genuine obstruction theory has richer coefficient systems and choices, but this table isolates the rule the chapter uses repeatedly.

label: Thom And Gysin
notes: Tie Thom and Gysin to Euler-class obstruction. The exact sequence says that multiplication by the Euler class measures whether cohomology can pass through the sphere bundle in the expected way. The sphere table makes the section obstruction concrete: even-dimensional spheres have Euler multiple two, while odd-dimensional spheres show zero in this model.

label: Stable Viewpoint
notes: Shift to the stable viewpoint by describing suspension as a packaging operation. Stable splittings simplify spaces after suspension, and spectra record compatible suspension data across all degrees. The purpose is not to abandon unstable homotopy, but to expose patterns hidden by low-dimensional accidents.

label: Dold-Thom
notes: Focus the Dold-Thom branch on the infinite symmetric product. Passing from X to SP of X turns ordinary integral homology into homotopy groups, so pi i of SP of X equals H i of X for connected CW complexes. The sphere check gives the clean model K of Z and n.

label: Steenrod And Adem
notes: Use the Adem table as a small algebra engine. Steenrod operations are stable cohomology operations, and Adem relations reduce non-admissible products to standard words or zero. The four displayed samples show how relations impose constraints that ordinary cohomology groups alone would miss.

label: Recap Exercise
notes: Close with an inspection exercise rather than a summary slogan. Ask students to choose a map or bundle and decide which machine applies first: exact sequence, CW compression, range theorem, fibration lifting, Postnikov obstruction, Thom-Gysin, or Steenrod algebra. The chapter is a toolbox, but each tool has hypotheses.
